title: Chhengthung Fa Takes the Manikya Name

title_i18n.en: Chhengthung Fa Takes the Manikya Name

subtitle: How a Hill Chief Forged the Ruby Line of Tripura
era: Foundation of the Manikya kingdom, c. 1400-1431 CE
region: Tripura hills between Sylhet, Comilla and Chittagong
moral: A kingdom begins when scattered peoples accept a shared standard.

sources.citation: Rajmala, first canto, compiled under Dharma Manikya I
sources.note: Primary dynastic narrative for the founder, but retrospective and partly legendary.

sources.citation: Ming Shilu, 15th-century references to Tripura as Di-wu-la
sources.note: External annalistic evidence for an early Tripura polity.

sources.citation: Ramani Mohan Sarma, History of the Kingdom of Tripura (1987); N.N. Bhattacharyya, Coinage of the Tripura Rajas (1986)
sources.note: Modern chronology correcting the Rajmala with numismatic evidence.

dialogue.text: In the misty hills between Bengal and the sea, Chhengthung Fa took the name Manikya—and turned a scattered land into a kingdom that would endure for centuries.
Around 1400, the Tripura hills were a patchwork of clans and clearings, jhum fields and bamboo forts, balanced between the forested uplands and the rich, restless plains of Bengal.

Rajmala, the court chronicle, remembers Chhengthung Fa as a hill chief among chiefs, born into the line that claimed these ridges, yet still needing to persuade rival Tripuri houses to follow his standard.

dialogue.speaker: chhengthung_fa
dialogue.text: If we stand apart, the hills will fall one village at a time.

The Rajmala says he subdued Kukis, Jamatias, Reangs—tribal polities along the ridges. Whether through battle, alliance, or both, later memory insists that under him the hill peoples began to march under one authority.
War left scars, but the chronicle speaks more of outcomes than details: ridges once independent accepted tribute, and a single court began to speak for the hills to the world beyond.

To the west lay the Bengal Sultanate, with cavalry, coins, and chroniclers. Between their plains and his hills, grazing and trade routes became lines of friction the Rajmala would later call a frontier incident.

The dynasty’s memory says that after a clash on this border, a Bengal Sultanate force came into the hills. No Bengal chronicler confirms it, yet in Tripura’s own record this threat looms over his story.

Rajmala tells of battle: Bengal cavalry pressing into unfamiliar forests, hill archers and spearmen using ridges and ravines. The details are legend, but the memory that hills could resist plains power became central to Tripura’s pride.

dialogue.speaker: chhengthung_fa
dialogue.text: Let the forest fight for us.

The Rajmala gives the victory to Chhengthung Fa. However we weigh its accuracy, by the time the chronicle was written, this story marked the moment the hills claimed parity with their powerful neighbor.

Then everything changed in the way he was named. Later coins and scholars like N.N. Bhattacharyya show that the Manikya title, tied to the image of a ruby, emerged with these early rulers, not only with the later Ratna Manikya.

dialogue.speaker: chhengthung_fa
dialogue.text: A name must bind more strongly than fear.
Rajmala remembers him as Maha Manikya—the Great Manikya. Whether the word came from a literal ruby or a metaphor for precious authority, it turned a hill chief into the founder of a named dynasty.

Centuries later, historians like Ramani Mohan Sarma would study these coins. Their inscriptions quietly correct the Rajmala’s ordering, revealing that the Manikya name was already in use before the more famous Ratna.

Beyond legend, external eyes also noticed. Ming Shilu, the Chinese imperial record, later spoke of Di-wu-la—Tripura—signaling that a polity in these hills was dealing with distant courts as well as nearby sultanates.

Chhengthung Fa’s life recedes in mist; his dates are pieced together from coins, chronicles, and echoes. But the kingdom he named would carry the Manikya title down five centuries of wars, alliances, and changing worlds.

In the end, his story is less about one man than about a moment when scattered hill peoples accepted a shared ruby name—and discovered that a standard, once raised, can outlast the hand that first held it.
